entries.question: Avery attacks with a [Guile] that was turned face-down by [Ixidron], and Nelson blocks with [Jerrard of the Closed Fist]. Does Avery shuffle?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude that Guile's "from anywhere" triggered ability will trigger after it dies face-down and return it to the library, so Avery shuffles.
entries.answer:
Direct answer stands: yes, Avery shuffles Guile into their library — but that conclusion rests entirely on the card data and rulings you gave me, not on the numbered Comprehensive Rules excerpts.

Being plain about the citations: every numbered rule in the provided context concerns declaring attackers, banding/"bands with other" (508.1e, 702.22c–m, 802.3b), and redundancy of menace/shadow/melee/soulbond. None of those address face-down creatures, evasion like "can't be blocked except by three or more creatures," combat damage, or dies/put-into-graveyard triggers. So the numbered rules text I was given does not settle this question; I am not going to attach an unrelated rule number to it.

What the provided card data does settle:
- Turned face down by Ixidron, Guile is a 2/2 with no name, no text, no subtypes, and no mana cost [Ixidron ruling #4]. So it lacks "can't be blocked except by three or more creatures," and Nelson's single blocker Jerrard of the Closed Fist is a legal block.
- Jerrard of the Closed Fist is 6/5 and deals 6 damage to the 2/2 face-down Guile, destroying it; the 2/2 deals only 2 back, so Jerrard of the Closed Fist survives.
- Guile's third ability triggers when Guile is put into a graveyard from anywhere and triggers from the graveyard itself, not as a leaves-the-battlefield ability [Guile ruling #0], [Guile ruling #5]. Losing the ability earlier (while face down on the battlefield) doesn't stop it; only lacking it while in the graveyard would [Guile ruling #7]. In the graveyard the card is Guile again, so it triggers and Avery shuffles it into their library.

Timing assumption: Guile was face down when combat damage was dealt. If it had been turned face up before blockers were declared, the single block by Jerrard of the Closed Fist would have been illegal.

Player count doesn't change any of this.

entries.answer_gold:
Yes. By default, triggered abilities are checked immediately after the event in question to see if they should trigger. At that point, the Guile is face-up in the graveyard and has that ability.

(Guile's trigger does not fit the exception for "leaves-the-battlefield" triggers because it is a "from anywhere" trigger.)

entries.question: Archer attacks with a [The Scarab God] that was turned face-down by [Ixidron] and Nia blocks with [Scathe Zombies]. Does The Scarab God trigger?

entries.answer:
No. While The Scarab God is face down because of Ixidron, it is a 2/2 creature with no text, no name, no subtypes, and no mana cost, so it simply has no abilities — neither the upkeep drain/scry trigger nor the "When The Scarab God dies, return it to its owner's hand" trigger exists to trigger [Ixidron ruling #4].

In the combat described, Archer's face-down The Scarab God (a 2/2) is blocked by Nia's Scathe Zombies (a 2/2). Each deals 2 damage to the other, so both are destroyed. Because the face-down permanent had no death-triggered ability at the time it left the battlefield, nothing triggers, and it does not come back to Archer's hand at the beginning of the next end step; it just stays in the graveyard (where it is again face up as The Scarab God card). Only a creature can attack or block, and only a player, planeswalker, or battle can be attacked, which the face-down 2/2 satisfies fine as an attacker [506.3].

Assumption on timing: I'm reading this as The Scarab God still being face down throughout the combat damage step. If instead it were somehow turned face up before it died (Ixidron leaving the battlefield does not by itself turn it face up, but another effect could), it would then have its printed abilities and its death trigger would work normally, returning it to Archer's hand at the beginning of the next end step [The Scarab God ruling #1].

This answer is the same whether the game has two players or more; nothing here depends on the number of opponents, though in a multiplayer game Archer would announce which opponent, planeswalker, or battle each attacker is attacking [508.1b].

entries.answer_gold: No. By default, triggered abilities are checked immediately after the event in question to see if they should trigger. However, "leaves-the-battlefield" triggers check the game state immediately before the event instead. At that point, The Scarab God had no abilities.

entries.question: Alaia casts [Biogenic Upgrade] targeting [Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11]. In total how many counters are be placed on Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11?
entries.reason: Both conclude nine +1/+1 counters are placed because Michelangelo's replacement effect adds one to each placement (3→4, then the doubling places 4 which becomes 5), totaling 9.
entries.answer:
Nine +1/+1 counters total are placed, leaving Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11 with nine +1/+1 counters (assuming it had none before).

Step by step:

1. Biogenic Upgrade distributes three +1/+1 counters to its single target, Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11. Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11's own static ability ("If one or more +1/+1 counters would be put on a creature you control, that many plus one +1/+1 counters are put on it instead") is a replacement effect that applies to this event, so four counters are put on instead of three. Card text like this governs over the plain instruction on Biogenic Upgrade.
2. Biogenic Upgrade then doubles the number of +1/+1 counters on it. Per [Biogenic Upgrade ruling #2], doubling means putting a number of +1/+1 counters on it equal to the number it already has — that's four — and "other cards that interact with putting counters on it will interact with this effect accordingly." So Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11's replacement effect applies again: four plus one = five counters are put on.

Total counters put on: 4 + 5 = 9, ending at nine +1/+1 counters (so a 10/10 base 1/1 becomes 10/10).

Notes: if Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11 already had counters, redo the doubling with that starting number and still add one extra to each placement. If you controlled a second copy, each would add one per placement ([Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11 ruling #3]), and if multiple counter-modifying effects applied you'd choose their order ([Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11 ruling #1], consistent with [616.1e]). None of this depends on player count, so it's the same in two-player and multiplayer games.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Nine. Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11's ability is a replacement effect that applies whenever counters are being placed on it When Biogenic Upgrade begins resolving, that replacement effect will add a counter, resulting in Alaia placing four +1/+1 counters. Afterwards, Biogenic Upgrade will then double the amount of counters on Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11. This results in an additional four counters being placed on it, which will then be modified by Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11's replacement effect again, resulting in nine +1/+1 counters in total.

entries.question: Addison casts [Ferocious Zheng]. After it resolves, they cast [Elemental Eruption] and reveal [Everdream] from their hand, splicing it onto Elemental Eruption. entries.answer:
Direct answer: Yes. Each storm copy of Elemental Eruption will also have Everdream spliced onto it, and Addison doesn't pay Everdream's {2}{U} splice cost again for the copies.

Important caveat about grounding: the numbered Comprehensive Rules excerpts I was given cover mana symbols, mana pools, cost reduction, and characteristic layers — none of them address splice, storm, or copying casting choices. So this answer rests entirely on the authoritative card rulings supplied with the card data, not on the provided numbered rules:

- [Everdream ruling #4] — if a spell is copied, choices made while casting it are copied, so the copy has the same cards spliced onto it as the original. Splicing Everdream onto Elemental Eruption is exactly such a choice.
- [Everdream ruling #1] — the spliced effect happens last, so each copy first creates the 4/4 red Dragon Elemental token with flying and prowess, then draws a card.

Count of copies: storm copies Elemental Eruption for each spell cast before it this turn. With only Ferocious Zheng cast beforehand, that's one copy (one extra token, one extra card drawn). This is player-count independent in principle — storm counts spells cast earlier in the turn regardless of who cast them, so at a multiplayer table there may simply be more copies, each still carrying Everdream.

entries.answer_gold: Yes. As Addison is casting Elemental Eruption they choose whether they want to splice as part of the casting process. When the storm trigger resolves it copies all the choices made when casting the original spell, including the choice to splice.

entries.question: Norah controls [Blood Sun]. Ari plays [Dark Depths] and then destroys the Blood Sun with [Sultai Charm]. What happens?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Dark Depths entered with no ice counters while Blood Sun was active, and when Blood Sun is destroyed Dark Depths' ability triggers and Ari sacrifices it to create the Marit Lage token.
entries.answer:
Ari ends up sacrificing Dark Depths and getting the 20/20 Marit Lage token.

Step by step:

1. While Norah's Blood Sun is on the battlefield, all lands lose all abilities except mana abilities. Dark Depths' "enters with ten ice counters" ability modifies how it enters the battlefield, and per [Blood Sun ruling #5] Dark Depths loses that ability before it can apply. So Dark Depths enters the battlefield with zero ice counters on it. (Dark Depths has no mana ability at all, so nothing of it survives Blood Sun — see [Dark Depths ruling #0].)
2. Dark Depths' last ability, "When Dark Depths has no ice counters on it, sacrifice it...", is a state trigger ([Dark Depths ruling #1]). While Blood Sun is on the battlefield, Dark Depths doesn't have that ability (it isn't a mana ability), so nothing triggers, and its {3} ability is likewise gone ([Blood Sun ruling #3] — a mana ability is one that produces mana, not one that costs mana).
3. Ari casts Sultai Charm choosing "Destroy target artifact or enchantment" targeting Blood Sun. Once Blood Sun leaves the battlefield, its continuous ability stops applying and Dark Depths immediately has its printed abilities again.
4. Because Dark Depths is on the battlefield with no ice counters on it, the state trigger's condition is already true, so it triggers right away. When it resolves, Ari sacrifices Dark Depths and creates Marit Lage, a legendary 20/20 black Avatar creature token with flying and indestructible. Note counters are not characteristics ([109.3]), but the trigger keys off the counters, not off characteristics — the point is simply that no ice counters were ever placed.

One caveat: if Dark Depths somehow leaves the battlefield before that triggered ability resolves, Ari can't sacrifice it and no token is created ([Dark Depths ruling #2]).

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Dark Depths entered while Blood Sun was already on the battlefield, as stated. If instead Dark Depths had entered first and Blood Sun arrived later, Dark Depths would already have its ten ice counters, and losing its abilities would just mean Ari can't remove counters with the {3} ability while Blood Sun remains — no free Marit Lage.

This interaction doesn't depend on player count; it plays out the same in two-player and multiplayer games (only the choice of legal targets for Sultai Charm can differ).

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Dark Depths entered the battlefield with no ice counters, since it didn't have the ability that would cause it to enter with them. When Blood Sun is destroyed, Dark Depths triggers since it has no ice counters on it and creates a Marit Lage token.

entries.question: Aiden controls [Volrath's Shapeshifter] and [Yixlid Jailer]. The top card of their graveyard is [Mistform Skyreaver]. Does Volrath's Shapeshifter have flying?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion and core reasoning as the reference: Volrath's Shapeshifter copies the Mistform Skyreaver's text (including flying) onto the battlefield, and Yixlid Jailer only strips abilities in the graveyard, not the card text that Shapeshifter copies.
entries.answer:
Yes — Volrath's Shapeshifter has flying (and is a 6/6 Illusion named Mistform Skyreaver with the {1}: change creature type ability, plus its own "{2}: Discard a card").

Why Yixlid Jailer doesn't stop this:
- Yixlid Jailer says "Cards in graveyards lose all abilities." That strips the functional abilities of the Mistform Skyreaver card while it sits in the graveyard, but it does not erase or rewrite that card's text.
- Volrath's Shapeshifter's own ability is what's doing the work here, and it functions from the battlefield, not from the graveyard, so Yixlid Jailer doesn't turn it off. That ability is a text-changing effect [Volrath's Shapeshifter ruling #5]: it gives Volrath's Shapeshifter "the full text of that card," i.e. Mistform Skyreaver's name, mana cost {5}{U}{U}, color (blue), types (Creature — Illusion), abilities as printed (flying; {1}: This creature becomes the creature type of your choice until end of turn), and power/toughness 6/6 [Volrath's Shapeshifter ruling #1]. Because the copied text is applied to Volrath's Shapeshifter on the battlefield, the flying ability exists there, where Yixlid Jailer has no effect.
- Volrath's Shapeshifter also keeps the granted "{2}: Discard a card" ability in addition to the copied abilities [Volrath's Shapeshifter ruling #1].

A useful parallel: Yixlid Jailer's own ruling notes that "enters the battlefield with" abilities are stripped in the graveyard but still apply once the card is actually on the battlefield, because what matters is having the ability where it functions [Yixlid Jailer ruling #3]. Same principle here — the flying text matters on the battlefield.

What Yixlid Jailer would change: any ability of Mistform Skyreaver that would need to function from the graveyard itself (a graveyard-activated ability like scavenge or embalm, or a graveyard trigger) is shut off [702.97a], [702.128a], [Yixlid Jailer ruling #4]. Mistform Skyreaver has no such abilities, so nothing is lost.

Also note this doesn't involve any "enters" event — changing forms doesn't trigger enters abilities [Volrath's Shapeshifter ruling #4]. None of this depends on the number of players; the answer is the same in two-player and multiplayer games.

entries.answer_gold: Yes. Yixlid Jailer only removes abilities, not text, and text is what Volrath's Shapeshifter cares about. Volrath's Shapeshifter also gains the text of the Mistform Skyreaver before Yixlid Jailer removes the abilities.

entries.question: Autumn controls [Bridge from Below] and [Silvercoat Lion]. They cast [Hour of Revelation]. Do they create a Zombie token?
entries.reason: Both conclude no token is created because Bridge from Below was on the battlefield (not in the graveyard) immediately before Hour of Revelation destroyed the creatures, so its ability doesn't trigger.
entries.answer:
No — Autumn does not create a Zombie token.

Grounding from the provided rules: Bridge from Below's own text conditions both triggered abilities on "if this card is in your graveyard," and rule [113.6k] explains that abilities of non-instant/sorcery objects function only where they can — a trigger condition that can't trigger from the battlefield functions in the zones it can trigger from, which for Bridge from Below is the graveyard. Card text overrides any general expectation here: Bridge from Below only does anything from a graveyard, and while it is on the battlefield it has no effect [Bridge from Below ruling #1].

Applied to your situation: Hour of Revelation destroys all nonland permanents, so Bridge from Below and Silvercoat Lion are put into Autumn's graveyard simultaneously. Bridge from Below was not in Autumn's graveyard immediately before Silvercoat Lion died, so its first ability doesn't trigger at all, and even if it had triggered it would need to still be in the graveyard on resolution to make a token [Bridge from Below ruling #0]. Its second ability likewise cares only about which graveyard the dead creature went to, not who controlled it [Bridge from Below ruling #3].

Secondary points:
- Cost note: Hour of Revelation costs {3}{W}{W}{W}; with ten or more nonland permanents on the battlefield when the cost is determined, it costs {W}{W}{W} — only the {3} generic portion is reduced, never the three {W} symbols [Hour of Revelation ruling #0].
- Multiplayer: same result with two players or more. Opponents' creatures destroyed by Hour of Revelation go to their own graveyards, but Bridge from Below still wasn't in Autumn's graveyard beforehand, so nothing triggers [Bridge from Below ruling #0]. Had Bridge from Below already been in Autumn's graveyard, Autumn could order simultaneous triggers to create a token before exiling Bridge from Below [Bridge from Below ruling #2].

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Leaves-the-battlefield triggers care about the state of the game immediately before the event in question. Bridge from Below was on the battlefield at that time, and won't trigger.

entries.question: Aspen controls [Parallel Lives] and a [Caldera Hellion]. They cast [Rite of Replication] targeting the Caldera Hellion. Can Aspen apply the devour replacement effect before the Parallel Lives replacement effect, sacrificing 1 creature to have each token enter with a +1/+1 counter?

entries.answer:
No. Aspen must apply Parallel Lives first, and only then the devour replacement effects of the tokens.

Why: creating a token is the outer event, and a permanent entering the battlefield is an event contained within that creation event. When one replacement effect applies to an event and another applies to an event contained within it, the outer one must be chosen first — so Parallel Lives (which replaces the number of tokens created) is applied before any "as this enters" replacement effect such as devour on the resulting tokens [616.1g]. Parallel Lives doubles the tokens: unkicked Rite of Replication makes 1 token, so 2 tokens; kicked (the additional {5}) it makes 5, so 10 tokens [Parallel Lives, Rite of Replication].

Then each token that's a copy of Caldera Hellion has its own devour 1, and each one's "as this creature enters" ability works on the token [Rite of Replication ruling #11]. But sacrificing one creature cannot feed all of them: the same object can't be chosen to change zones more than once when applying replacement effects that modify how permanents enter the battlefield [614.13b], and a creature you already control can be devoured by only one of several simultaneously-entering devour creatures [Caldera Hellion ruling #3]. So one sacrificed creature gives exactly one token a single +1/+1 counter; every other token enters with none. To give each token a counter you'd need one separate already-on-battlefield creature per token, and none of the entering tokens can be devoured, nor can a token devour itself [Caldera Hellion ruling #1]. All creatures devoured this way are sacrificed at the same time [Caldera Hellion ruling #3].

Note also that each token then triggers "deals 3 damage to each creature," and a token with only one +1/+1 counter (4/4) still dies to the combined damage from multiple tokens [Caldera Hellion ruling #4].

This analysis doesn't depend on player count; if more than two players are at the table and multiple players had simultaneous replacement choices, those choices would be made in APNAP order [616.1g].

entries.answer_gold: No. There are two replacement effects trying to apply to the original event of creating a Caldera Hellion: Caldera Hellion's own effect and Parallel Lives's effect. Caldera Hellion's effect applies to it entering the battlefield however, while Parallel Lives's effect applies to it being created, so Parallel Lives's effect must be applied first. After that is applied the original Caldera Hellion's effect doesn't exist anymore, but each of the new Caldera Hellions entering the battlefield has its own effect, which can now be applied individually.

Back from the Brink's ability requires exiling a creature card from your graveyard and paying its mana cost. Shifting Wall's mana cost is just {X}. Per [Back from the Brink ruling #3], if the exiled creature card has {X} in its mana cost, X is considered to be zero — Adelyn doesn't get to choose a larger value, so the total paid is {0} and there is no way to pay more.

Shifting Wall's own text says "This creature enters with X +1/+1 counters on it." That "enters with" ability does apply to the token ([Back from the Brink ruling #2] confirms "as [this creature] enters" and "[this creature] enters with" abilities work), but with X = 0 it enters with zero +1/+1 counters. Since Shifting Wall's printed power/toughness is 0/0, the token is a 0/0 creature and will be put into the graveyard as a state-based action for having 0 toughness essentially immediately.

Note also that the token copy has defender, which means it can't attack ([702.3b]), so it would only ever be useful as a blocker — and at 0/0 with no counters it won't survive to block anyway. Nothing here depends on the number of players.

entries.question: Alex controls a [Krark-Clan Ironworks], a [Mycosynth Lattice], and a [Control Magic] that took control of a [Boris Devilboon] from Nico. Alex begins activating the ability of Boris Devilboon and sacrifices Control Magic to help pay the cost. Is this legal? If so, who will control the ability?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude the activation is legal and that Alex controls the ability on the stack (so Alex gets the token), so the candidate reaches the same final ruling as the reference.
entries.answer:
Yes, it's legal, and Alex controls the ability (and gets the Minor Demon token).

Why sacrificing Control Magic works: Mycosynth Lattice says "All permanents are artifacts in addition to their other types," and that explicitly includes Auras — the ruling confirms "The Lattice's first ability causes Auras to become artifacts" [Mycosynth Lattice ruling #3]. So Control Magic, an Aura on the battlefield, is an artifact and is a legal thing to sacrifice to Krark-Clan Ironworks' cost "Sacrifice an artifact: Add {C}{C}." Note the mana produced is {C}{C} (colorless specifically), but Boris Devilboon's cost is {2}{B}{R}, {T} — the {2} is generic, so the two {C} pay that part; the {B} and {R} must still come from elsewhere, though Mycosynth Lattice's third ability ("Players may spend mana as though it were mana of any color") lets Alex spend colorless mana as though it were black or red, so the {C}{C} could instead pay {B}{R} if Alex has other mana for the generic {2}.

Why Alex keeps the ability: Alex controlled Boris Devilboon at the moment the ability was activated (Control Magic: "You control enchanted creature"), so Alex is the ability's controller, and the ability exists independently on the stack once activated. Sacrificing Control Magic during the payment of costs means Boris Devilboon immediately reverts to Nico's control (tapped, since {T} was paid), but that does not change who controls the already-activated ability or undo it. The token is created under Alex's control.

Timing note: I'm assuming Alex activates the ability first and sacrifices Control Magic while paying costs (as stated). If instead Control Magic were sacrificed before activation, Alex would no longer control Boris Devilboon and could not activate its ability at all.

One caveat on grounding: the specific numbered rules about who controls an activated ability and about paying costs after activation weren't included in the context provided to me; the answer above rests on the card texts and the Mycosynth Lattice ruling. Multiplayer: nothing changes with more than two players here — the only provided multiplayer rule concerns a player leaving the game, in which case an ability that would be controlled by a departed player isn't put on the stack [800.4d]; that doesn't apply while Alex is still in the game.

entries.answer_gold:
Yes, this is legal, and Alex will control the ability. The process for activating an ability is the same as the process for casting a spell. The first step of activating an ability is to put it onto the stack. Mana abilities are activated in a later step. The ability is already on the stack at this point (controlled by Alex), so the Boris Devilboon changing controllers won't change who controls the ability. After activating mana abilities, Alex must pay the activation cost. {T} means "tap this permanent", so Alex can pay the cost regardless of who controls the Boris Devilboon at that time.

Legality is checked before mana abilities are activated, so it won't matter that Boris Devilboon gets summoning sickness when it changes controllers.

entries.question: Nico has cast a [Gather Specimens] earlier in the turn. Aiden controls a [Chronatog Totem] that is currently a creature due to its own ability, and casts an [Evil Twin], choosing to have it copy Chronatog Totem. What happens?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same bottom-line ruling that Evil Twin enters under Nico's control and Nico (not Aiden) chooses what it copies as it enters the battlefield.
entries.answer:
Direct answer (unchanged in substance, but now stated with its actual grounding): Evil Twin enters the battlefield under Nico's control, and Nico — not Aiden — makes the copy choice.

Important caveat about sourcing: the numbered Comprehensive Rules excerpts I was given (about blight, amass, scavenge, embalm, graft, shuffling, layers, and state-based actions) do not address Gather Specimens, control-changing entry replacements, or copy effects. So this answer rests entirely on the card rulings provided as ground truth, not on the numbered rules text; if you want a rules-number citation, the relevant CR sections weren't supplied here.

From the provided card rulings:
- Gather Specimens isn't targeted and affects creatures that would enter under any opponent's control [Gather Specimens ruling #4], and it applies to creatures entering by any means, including resolving creature spells [Gather Specimens ruling #7]. Evil Twin is such a spell, so the permanent enters under Nico's control; casting choices are remembered and "enters" triggers happen after it's under Nico's control [Gather Specimens ruling #6].
- Gather Specimens' replacement effect is applied before other effects that modify how the creature enters, and the explicit example is that if Clone would enter under an opponent's control, you choose which creature it copies as it enters under your control [Gather Specimens ruling #3]. Evil Twin's "you may have this creature enter as a copy" is that same kind of effect, so Aiden's intent to copy Chronatog Totem is not binding — Nico chooses, and may choose nothing, in which case Evil Twin is a 0/0 and goes to the graveyard [Evil Twin ruling #4].
- If Nico does copy Chronatog Totem, only Chronatog Totem's printed copiable values are copied, not the non-copy effect that made it a creature until end of turn [Evil Twin ruling #7]. So it enters as a noncreature artifact named Chronatog Totem with its three abilities plus "{U}{B}, {T}: Destroy target creature with the same name as this creature" — it has no power/toughness and doesn't die. Even if Nico pays {1}{U} to animate it, it can't attack or use "{T}: Add {U}" this turn, because its controller must have controlled the permanent continuously since the beginning of their most recent turn [Chronatog Totem ruling #0].

Timing: I'm assuming Gather Specimens resolved before Evil Twin was cast, as stated; it doesn't retroactively change control of creatures that already entered [Gather Specimens ruling #0]. Had Gather Specimens come after Evil Twin entered, Evil Twin would stay under Aiden's control with Aiden's copy choice.

Multiplayer: same result with more than two players, since Gather Specimens hits creatures entering under any opponent's control [Gather Specimens ruling #4]; if multiple Gather Specimens were cast this turn, the would-be controller chooses which applies first and the process repeats [Gather Specimens ruling #5], which can leave the creature with its original controller when two opposing players each cast one [Gather Specimens ruling #8].

entries.answer_gold: This can't happen as described. As Evil Twin begins to resolve, Nico gains control of it before any other choices are made. Nico will make the choice of what to copy as it enters the battlefield.

entries.question: Albert and Nico are beginning the game and have just drawn 7 cards. Albert has [Serum Powder] in their hand. Does Albert get to know whether Nico is going to mulligan before deciding whether to use Serum Powder's ability?
entries.reason: The candidate calls the situation ambiguous and declines to state the order, whereas the reference clearly states Albert must decide (and exiles/draws) before Nico decides, so they reach different conclusions.
entries.answer:
The provided rules don't settle this. Nothing in the context includes the mulligan procedure (rule 103.4 and its steps), which is what governs the order in which players decide to mulligan and how much information each player has before deciding. Serum Powder's own text only tells us when Albert may use the ability — "Any time you could mulligan and this card is in your hand" — and its rulings only confirm that using it doesn't prevent further mulligans and that the exiled cards stay exiled for the game [Serum Powder ruling #0] [Serum Powder ruling #1].

The closest general principle in the context is the APNAP rule: when multiple players would make choices at the same time, the active player chooses first, then each other player in turn order, and a later player knows the choices already made [101.4b]. That would suggest whichever of Albert or Nico chooses second knows the earlier player's decision, but the mulligan step is not framed as a simultaneous-choice event by any rule given here, so applying [101.4b] to it would be a guess. Note also that the question involves two players (Albert and Nico); with more than two players the turn-order sequencing of such choices could matter more, but again the mulligan rules needed to say so aren't provided.

What's missing: the mulligan procedure rules (order of mulligan declarations and whether they're simultaneous or sequential).

entries.answer_gold: No. Albert exiles their hand and draws 7 cards at the time they would normally declare if they are going to take a mulligan, which is before Nico has made that decision.
